statement: As summarized by Sarparast et al. (2022), reports from people who took ecstasy together with prescribed medicines point to more harm with some combinations, but they cannot show cause. In 946 reports of recreational ecstasy use to the US adverse event reporting system between 2000 and 2020 (mean age 28; 70.1% men), reports that also named an antidepressant had higher odds of a fatal outcome than reports that did not (adjusted odds ratio 1.62, against 8.17 for muscle relaxants, 7.13 for anesthetics, 3.05 for amphetamines and stimulants, 2.25 for benzodiazepines, 2.05 for opioids and 2.03 for alcohol); without adjustment the odds ratios were 2.82 for bupropion, 2.36 for sertraline, 1.97 for venlafaxine, 1.92 for citalopram and 1.86 for olanzapine, all 18 reports that named metoclopramide ended in death, and no death was reported with risperidone or lithium (Cohen et al., 2021). In a survey of 216 adults who had taken ecstasy with a pharmaceutical drug in the previous 6 months, 76% of those who combined it with an antidepressant still felt euphoria, and they reported higher rates of muscle rigidity, involuntary eye movements, dizziness, headache and heavy sweating, but antidepressants were not separated by class and included monoamine-oxidase inhibitors (Copeland et al., 2006). The review gives no intervals, no numbers of deaths and no denominators; voluntary reports cannot show how many people took each combination, what else they took, or how much; and neither study was read for this library. The review's authors suggest, without data, that effects blunted by an SSRI may lead some people to take more, which could explain the higher odds.
plain: Besides lab studies, there are reports. In a US database of voluntary reports about ecstasy (946 reports), the ones that also named an antidepressant ended in death more often than those that did not. In a survey of 216 adults, people who mixed ecstasy with an antidepressant still felt euphoria, and reported more sweating, headache, dizziness and muscle stiffness. Reports cannot show cause: nobody knows how many people took each mix, what else they took, or how much. The review's authors guess that people who feel little may take more, but no data show it. Both studies come second-hand, from a 2022 review.
population: People who took ecstasy together with prescribed medicines: 946 reports to a US adverse event reporting system (2000 to 2020; mean age 28; 70.1% men) and 216 adults in a cross-sectional survey (mean age 26; 63% men; mean 11 days of ecstasy use in 6 months), as summarized by Sarparast et al. (2022)
exposure: Taking ecstasy together with an antidepressant, or with another named prescribed medicine, as reported (no doses or timing given)
comparator: Reports or respondents involving ecstasy without that medicine
outcome: A fatal outcome in a report (odds ratios); euphoria and physical symptoms in a survey
magnitude: Cohen et al. (2021), as summarized: fatal outcome, adjusted odds ratio with a drug class also named: antidepressants 1.62, benzodiazepines 2.25, opioids 2.05, ethanol 2.03, amphetamines and stimulants 3.05, anesthetics 7.13, muscle relaxants 8.17; unadjusted odds ratios: bupropion 2.82, sertraline 2.36, venlafaxine 1.97, citalopram 1.92, olanzapine 1.86; metoclopramide 18 of 18 reports fatal; risperidone and lithium no deaths. No intervals, deaths or denominators given. Copeland et al. (2006), as summarized: among people combining ecstasy with antidepressants, 76% still felt euphoria; higher rates of muscle rigidity, nystagmus, dizziness, headache and heavy sweating (percentages in the review are paired without labels).

evidence.extracted: Surveillance study (Cohen et al., 2021, as summarized here): 946 unique reports of recreational ecstasy use in the US adverse-event database, 2000-2020 (mean age 28, 70.1% men). Adjusted odds ratios of a fatal outcome when a drug class was also reported: MDMA metabolites or analogs 8.71, muscle relaxants 8.17, anesthetics 7.13, amphetamines and stimulants 3.05, benzodiazepines 2.25, opioids 2.05, ethanol 2.03, antidepressants 1.62. Unadjusted odds ratios for single psychiatric medicines: bupropion 2.82, sertraline 2.36, venlafaxine 1.97, citalopram 1.92, olanzapine 1.86; all 18 reports with metoclopramide ended in death; risperidone and lithium odds ratios could not be calculated because there were no deaths. No intervals, numbers of deaths or denominators are given.

Survey (Copeland et al., 2006, as summarized here): 216 adults who took ecstasy with a pharmaceutical drug in the past 6 months (mean age 26, 63% men, mean 11 days of ecstasy use in 6 months). Of those who took antidepressants with ecstasy, 76% still felt euphoria, but rates of muscle rigidity (0% vs 45%), nystagmus (0% vs 33%), dizziness (19% vs 42%), headache (21% vs 62%) and heavy sweating (28% vs 53%) were higher; antidepressants were not analysed by class and included MAOIs. Group sizes and the order of the paired percentages are not stated.

evidence.locator: Discussion › Trends in case studies, 1st paragraph; Discussion › Considerations for future research, 3rd paragraph
evidence.extracted: The review's authors write that the blunted subjective effects of SSRIs may lead people to take escalating doses and so explain the higher odds of death in the surveillance data, and that benzodiazepines were associated with a higher adjusted odds ratio of death than antidepressants, opioids or alcohol; no data on amounts taken are given. The review found no study of benzodiazepines with MDMA, and notes that the surveillance study concerns unregulated ecstasy use in non-clinical settings.
evidence.quote: may drive individuals to take escalating drug doses to achieve effects

risk_of_bias.note: Voluntary adverse-event reports and a retrospective survey; no denominators, no way to know what else was taken; individual-medicine odds ratios are unadjusted.

inconsistency.note: Not rated: the two studies measure different outcomes.

indirectness.note: Second-hand: neither study was read; the review gives no intervals, counts or class sizes, and the paired survey percentages are unlabelled.

imprecision.note: No intervals; small numbers behind several odds ratios cannot be seen.

grade.reasoning: Observational reports start low (METHODS 6.3); risk of bias, indirectness and imprecision each take a level, and the result is very low. Status single-study: each outcome rests on one study. Stays at draft because it rests only on the review as summarized (METHODS 12, brief). The claim is worded as an association in reports and states that cause, amounts and denominators are unknown; it gives no advice.

verification.flag_note: Rests only on Sarparast et al. (2022) as summarized. No reference records exist for Cohen et al. (2021, Sci Rep, doi 10.1038/s41598-021-85389-x) or Copeland et al. (2006, Addict Behav, doi 10.1016/j.addbeh.2005.05.025); build them, read them, and replace these second-hand anchors. Reader 56's claim on deaths involving MDMA and medicines (coroners' cases) covers related ground; the editor may join them.
